tips.title: O and a: every noun is masculine or feminine
body: Every Portuguese noun is masculine or feminine, and “the” changes to match: o for masculine, a for feminine.
Words ending in -o are usually masculine and words ending in -a usually feminine. “My” matches too: meu gato, minha casa.

tips.title: No need for “he”, “she” or “I”
body: The verb's ending already says who it is, so Brazilians often drop eu (I) when it's clear: “Tenho uma irmã” is as natural as “Eu tenho uma irmã”.
É on its own means “he is”, “she is” or “it is”: “É meu irmão.”

tips.title: Adjectives go after the noun and match it
body: Most describing words come after the noun: a casa pequena, “the small house”.
They change to match: pequeno for a masculine noun, pequena for a feminine one, and add -s for more than one.

tips.title: Estou com fome: “I'm with hunger”
body: To say you're hungry or sleepy, Brazilians use estar com (to be with): estou com fome, estou com sono.
The same works for cold (estou com frio), heat (estou com calor) and thirst (estou com sede).

tips.title: Quero + a verb: “I want to…”
body: Put the verb straight after quero, with no extra word for “to”: quero brincar, “I want to play”.
For a polite question, Brazilians use você: “Você quer água?” To say no, put não in front: “Não quero.”

tips.title: Gostar de: you like “of” something
body: Gostar always takes de: “Eu gosto de chocolate.” De joins the next word: de + o = do, de + a = da.
“Gosto do Brasil” (I like Brazil), “gosto da praia” (I like the beach). Adorar (to love) needs no de.

tips.title: Asking questions
body: Often a question is just a sentence said with a rising voice: “Você quer água?”
Question words: o que (what), quem (who), onde (where), por que (why), quanto (how much). In speech, “cadê?” is a casual “where is?”

tips.title: Estar for where things are
body: Use estar for where something is right now: “O livro está na mesa.”
Em (in, on) joins o and a: em + o = no, em + a = na. Fixed places (a city, a building) often use ficar: “Onde fica o banheiro?”

tips.title: Telling someone what to do
body: For directions, Brazilians use the polite command form: vire (turn), siga (go on), pegue (take).
Between friends you'll also hear the everyday form: vira à esquerda, segue reto.

tips.title: Ser or estar?
body: Portuguese has two verbs for “to be”. Ser is for what someone is: their job, where they're from, what they're like.
Estar is for how or where someone is right now: “Estou cansado” (I'm tired). Being married is usually ser casado.

tips.title: Você and o senhor
body: In Brazil, você is the everyday “you”, for friends and strangers alike. It uses the same verb form as ele and ela: “você tem”.
To be extra polite, especially with older people, say o senhor (to a man) or a senhora (to a woman).

tips.title: Eu queria: a softer “I want”
body: When ordering, “eu queria” (I would like, literally “I wanted”) sounds polite. “Quero” is fine but more direct.
“Para mim…” (for me…) is the easy way to order: “Para mim, o frango.”

tips.title: Me visto: verbs you do to yourself
body: Some verbs come with me, te or se when you do them to yourself: eu me visto (I get dressed), ele se levanta (he gets up).
In Brazil the me goes before the verb in speech: “Eu me chamo Ana.”

tips.title: The past: what happened
body: For things that happened and finished, use the simple past: fui (I went), fiz (I did), almocei (I had lunch).
Regular verbs: -ar verbs end in -ei (almocei), -er verbs in -i (comi), -ir verbs in -i (dormi).

tips.title: Two past tenses: the scene and the event
body: The imperfect sets the scene or says what used to happen: ela morava (she lived), andava (she would walk).
The simple past tells what happened once: ela encontrou (she found). Stories mix the two.

tips.title: Had done: tinha + -ado / -ido
body: To say something had already happened before another past moment, use tinha with the participle: tinha saído (had left).
Enquanto (while) with the imperfect sets the background: “Enquanto eu cozinhava, o telefone tocou.”

tips.title: Plans: vou + verb, and a gente
body: Vou + a verb is the easy future: vou reservar (I'm going to book).
Brazilians often say a gente for “we”, with the verb like ele: “a gente se encontra”, “a gente fica em casa”.

tips.title: Saying what hurts
body: “Estou com dor de…” (I have a pain in…): estou com dor de cabeça, dor de garganta (sore throat).
Or point and say “Dói aqui” (it hurts here). Desde means “since”: “febre desde ontem”.

tips.title: Giving advice: deveria, se eu fosse você, and the subjunctive
body: “Você deveria…” (you should…) is gentle advice. “Se eu fosse você…” (if I were you…) uses a special past form.
After “recomendo que” or “é importante que”, the next verb changes to the subjunctive: durma, beba.

tips.title: Foi cancelado: the passive
body: Ser + participle says what was done to something: “O voo foi cancelado” (the flight was cancelled).
The participle matches the noun: a mala foi perdida, os voos foram cancelados.

tips.title: Acho que… / Não acho que…
body: “Acho que” (I think that) takes a normal verb: “Acho que você tem razão.”
With “não acho que” (I don't think), the next verb goes into the subjunctive: “Não acho que seja justo.”

tips.title: Linking ideas
body: Por um lado… por outro lado… (on the one hand… on the other…) lays out two sides.
“Mesmo que” (even if) takes the subjunctive: “Mesmo que seja difícil.” “No entanto” means “however”.

tips.title: Você or o senhor?
body: Brazilians switch to “você” quickly. With older people, customers or anyone you'd like to honor, start with o senhor / a senhora.
If they say “Pode me chamar de você”, you've been invited to be casual.

tips.title: Extra-polite requests
body: “Será que o senhor poderia…?” (would you possibly be able to…?) is very polite.
In shops and cafés, “Me vê um…, por favor?” (literally “see me a…”) is a friendly, natural way to ask.

tips.title: How people really talk: tô, tá, pra
body: In everyday speech, estou becomes tô, está becomes tá, and para becomes pra.
“Tô de boa”, “Tá bom”, “Pra quê?” You'll read them in messages and hear them everywhere.

tips.title: Culture: dating in Brazil
body: Brazilians are warm and direct: compliments and long eye contact are normal and friendly.
A “ficar” is a casual fling; “namorar” means you're officially dating. It's fine to ask which one it is.

tips.title: Culture: texting in Brazil
body: “Kkkkk” or “rsrs” is laughter in Brazilian texts. Voice messages (áudios) are hugely popular on WhatsApp.
“Sumido!” (stranger!) is a playful way to say you haven't heard from someone in a while.

tips.title: Culture: meeting the family
body: Family is central in Brazil, and Sunday lunch is a big event. Bring a small gift (uma lembrancinha), like dessert.
Call your partner's parents “seu” (Mr.) or “dona” (Mrs.) with their first name: dona Maria, seu João.

tips.title: Culture: paquera, Brazilian flirting
body: Paquerar is to flirt. Compliments about someone's smile, laugh or style land well when they're specific and genuine.
Keep it light and fun. If the other person stops playing along, change the subject kindly.

tips.title: Culture: zoeira, playful teasing
body: Brazilians love zoeira: friendly teasing and jokes. Being able to laugh at yourself goes a long way.
“Que convencido!” (someone's full of himself!) is teasing, not an insult, when said with a smile.

tips.title: Culture: clear and kind
body: Ask clearly and accept a no gracefully. “Respeito a sua resposta” says you're a good sport.
“Sem problema, foi um prazer” lets everyone leave with a smile.

tips.title: Culture: greetings in Brazil
body: Friends greet with a hug or a kiss on the cheek: one in São Paulo, two in Rio. Men often hug and pat each other's back.
“Tudo bem?” is a greeting, not a real question: answer “Tudo!” and ask back.

tips.title: Culture: at the table in Brazil
body: Lunch is the main meal: rice, beans, meat and salad (o prato feito, the set plate) is a classic.
In restaurants you usually have to ask for the check: “Pode fechar a conta?” The 10% service is suggested, not required.

tips.title: Culture: holidays in Brazil
body: On New Year's Eve (Réveillon) people wear white for peace and jump seven waves for luck. Carnival takes over the country for four days before Lent.
In June, festas juninas bring bonfires, country dancing (quadrilha) and corn treats like pamonha.

tips.title: Culture: mistakes foreigners make
body: Avoid the 👌 hand sign: in Brazil it's rude. A thumbs up 👍 is the friendly “OK”.
Watch false friends: esquisito is “weird”, puxar is “to pull” (not push), and pretender is “to intend”.

tips.title: Culture: Brazil and Portugal
body: Portugal and Brazil share a language but not all their words: ônibus / autocarro (bus), celular / telemóvel (phone), legal / fixe (cool).
Brazil's regions have their own flavor too: “bah, tchê” in the south, “trem” in Minas Gerais, “massa” in the northeast.
